source.title: Functional Scaling Laws in Kernel Regression: Loss Dynamics and Learning Rate Schedules
source.authors: Binghui Li; Fengling Chen; Zixun Huang; Lean Wang; Lei Wu

record.file_problem: none; the full paper text, including appendices, is present.
record.tranche_reason: The paper develops scaling results for power-law kernel regression and fits loss trajectories from LLM pretraining, but does not test the specified language-model scaling claims: its LLM experiments keep model size and token budget fixed while comparing learning-rate schedules. Its kernel-regression results are a different system, so they are recorded as related findings rather than as tests of the claim versions.
record.gate_note: The paper cites Kaplan and Hoffmann and presents theoretical scaling laws for power-law kernel regression. Its LLM experiments fit a trajectory on an 8-1-1 schedule and predict trajectories on other schedules at the same model size and token budget; this is not extrapolation across model sizes, tokens or compute. The paper does not report downstream-task performance, architecture-shape comparisons, or scaling-law fit dependence on LLM size. Cited results from other work are not recorded as rows.
record.test_reason: No result bears on any version as stated for language models. Its power-law, extrapolation and compute-optimal results are analytical derivations, plus SGD simulations, for power-law kernel regression, a different system. Its LLM experiments (0.1B–1B) hold model size fixed and drop the M term from the fit. They fit loss trajectories on one learning-rate schedule and predict others, or optimise the schedule. That is a related construct (schedule-dependent trajectory prediction), not loss scaling across parameters, tokens or compute. The paper claims consistency with Kaplan and Hoffmann (larger models more compute-efficient; data scaled more than model), but only inside the kernel model.
record.authors_conclusion: Mostly correct. The authors conclude that an intrinsic-time functional scaling law captures full SGD loss trajectories in power-law kernel regression under any schedule. It explains why decay helps, why WSD beats pure decay, and why higher-capacity models are more efficient, with compute-optimal training favouring data over model size. They also conclude that FSL is a useful surrogate for fitting, predicting and designing LLM schedules (0.1B–1B).
record.recipe_differences: The study develops an intrinsic-time functional scaling law for power-law kernel regression and fits it to LLM trajectories; it does not reproduce the original parameter/data scaling sweeps or compute-optimal allocation experiments.
record.method_sensitivity: The derived risk and compute-optimal scaling relations differ by learning-rate schedule and by easy versus hard task regime; the theoretical laws also depend on task difficulty s, capacity exponent β, label noise and schedule assumptions. LLM experiments compare architectures, sizes, training durations and schedules, but do not test how these choices change fitted size/token scaling exponents.

fits_no_version.finding: In power-law kernel regression, the theory says data- and compute-optimal exponents and splits change with the learning-rate schedule (constant < exp-decay < WSD) and with the easy/hard task regime. SGD simulations follow these predictions.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: In kernel-regression models of scaling, scaling exponents and compute-optimal allocation depend on the learning-rate schedule and task regime.

fits_no_version.finding: An FSL fitted on the 8-1-1 schedule predicts cosine and WSD loss trajectories for 400M and 1B LLaMA, and WSD for 100M GPT-2 (fit RMSE 0.019–0.038). It also fits trajectories of 100M LLaMA runs of 10B–80B tokens.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Fitted functional laws predict LLM loss trajectories across learning-rate schedules and training lengths at fixed model size.

fits_no_version.finding: FSL-optimal schedules (WSD-like, decaying below 0.1ηmax) give lower final loss than cosine, WSD and 8-1-1 on 1B QwenMoE, 1B LLaMA, 100M GPT-2 and 100M LLaMA. The gap over WSD variants is about 0.01 on 400M.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Schedules optimised under a fitted trajectory law beat standard schedules in LLM pretraining.

record.problems: The theoretical results concern a stylized power-law kernel-regression model and its continuous-time approximation. LLM evidence covers a limited set of sizes and fixed token budgets for schedule prediction, not size/token/compute scaling or downstream tasks. Many experimental outcomes are described qualitatively or shown in figures without numerical values or uncertainty estimates.
record.rows_left_out: No rows omitted for the 60-row limit.

untested.parts: No sweep of LLM held-out loss over parameters, tokens or compute. The M term is dropped in the LLM fits.
No extrapolation from small to much larger runs. Prediction is across schedules at fixed size and token budget.
Compute-optimal allocation is derived only for kernel regression; there is no LLM allocation experiment.
No comparison of depth or width at fixed parameter count.
No other modalities, repeated data, fine-tuning or transfer.
Schedule-dependence of exponents and of the compute-optimal split is shown only analytically for kernel regression. LLM exponent or allocation dependence on setup is not tested.

record.verdict_notes: Appendix B.2 reports further LLM results (Figs 4–9) that no row records: 100M GPT-2, 100M LLaMA at 17k–134k steps with RMSE about 0.09–0.11, and WSD decay-ratio variants. They bear on no version, so they are not listed as missing; they belong with the fits_no_version entries. Relation 'discusses' and tranche T6 are kept; it could be argued as T4/uses_without_test, but no claim version is tested either way.

versions.untested_parts: No sweep of LLM held-out pretraining loss against parameter count, tokens or compute; power-law results concern kernel-regression risk.
LLM predictions transfer between learning-rate schedules at the same size and token budget, not from small runs to runs orders of magnitude larger.
Compute-optimal allocations are derived for kernel regression, not tested on language models.
No controlled comparison of depth, width or other architecture details at fixed parameter count.
No experiments on other modalities, repeated data, fine-tuning or transfer.
No downstream-task results or analysis of downstream performance versus pretraining loss.

The paper derives schedule-dependent laws for kernel regression, but does not test whether LLM fitted exponents or compute-optimal allocations depend on counting, data, schedule or fitting choices, or whether LLM curves bend away from a single power law.
